title: Arc<T> is Send and Sync only when T already is

steps.title: Send and Sync are two separate questions
steps.line: Send: move it to another thread. Sync: share &T between threads.
steps.caption: Send asks whether a value can move to another thread. Sync asks whether several threads can hold a shared reference to it at once: the standard library defines T as Sync exactly when &T is Send. The compiler answers both for every type, so each type falls in one of four quadrants.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart; 6 labels.

steps.title: i32 is Send and Sync
steps.line: Auto traits: a type built from Send and Sync parts gets both.
steps.caption: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler gives them to any type built only from parts that have them. Primitives such as i32 have both, so i32 sits in the top-right quadrant. Each point sits at one fixed spot in its quadrant, so only the quadrant carries meaning.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; 4 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside i32. New in this step: i32; 4 labels.

steps.title: Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Rc counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one.
steps.caption: Rc counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one. Two threads cloning Rcs that share one count could update it at the same moment, which is undefined behaviour. So rc.rs declares Rc neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 2 points; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside Rc<i32>. New in this step: Rc<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: Cell<i32> can move but cannot be shared
steps.line: Cell::set takes &self and does no synchronisation: not Sync.
steps.caption: Cell::set takes &self and does no synchronisation, so two threads holding &Cell could write to it at once. That is why cell.rs makes Cell not Sync. It still makes Cell<T> Send whenever T is, so a whole Cell can move to another thread.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 3 points; 1 label. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: no” beside Cell<i32>. New in this step: Cell<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: MutexGuard<i32> can be shared but cannot move
steps.line: Dropping it must unlock on the thread that locked: not Send.
steps.caption: Dropping a MutexGuard unlocks its mutex, and with POSIX threads a lock must be released on the thread that took it, so mutex.rs makes the guard not Send. A shared &MutexGuard gives out &i32, so mutex.rs makes the guard Sync when the value inside is Sync.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 4 points; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: yes” beside MutexGuard<i32>. New in this step: MutexGuard<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: Arc needs Send and Sync inside; Mutex needs Send
steps.line: Arc clones on several threads reach one T with no added safety.
steps.caption: Arc<T> is Send or Sync only when T is both: clones of one Arc on several threads all reach the same T, and Arc adds no thread safety to it. Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, because its lock lets one thread at a time use the value. The lines omit ?Sized and the allocator.
steps.picture: Code, 6 lines; 1 label. This wrapper: 2: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Send for Arc<T> {}; 3: unsafe impl<T: Send + Sync> Sync for Arc<T> {}.

steps.title: Arc<i32> is Send and Sync
steps.line: Arc needs T: Send + Sync; i32 is Send and Sync.
steps.caption: Wrapping i32 in Arc gives Arc<i32>. Arc needs the type inside to be both Send and Sync, and i32 is Send and Sync, so Arc<i32> is Send and Sync. The point stays in “Send and Sync”.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; 2 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside x is Arc<i32>.

steps.title: Both thread APIs accept x
steps.line: Here x is Send and Sync: spawn needs Send, scope Sync.
steps.caption: thread::spawn needs a Send closure, and a move closure that owns x is Send only if Arc<i32> is. thread::scope lets threads borrow &x instead, and a closure holding &x is Send only if Arc<i32> is Sync. rustc 1.99.1 accepts both for x: Arc<i32>.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; “Compiles?”, 2 labelled values; 2 labels. Accepted: x is Arc<i32>. New in this step: “Compiles?”, 2 labelled values; 2 labels.

steps.line: With T: Send, Mutex<T> is Send and Sync, as Arc needs.
steps.caption: Arc<T> is Send or Sync only when T is both: clones of one Arc on several threads all reach the same T, and Arc adds no thread safety to it. Mutex<T> needs only T: Send, because its lock lets one thread at a time use the value. The lines omit ?Sized and the allocator.

steps.title: Send and Sync are two separate questions
steps.line: Send: move it to another thread. Sync: share &T between threads.
steps.caption: Send asks whether a value can move to another thread. Sync asks whether several threads can hold a shared reference to it at once: the standard library defines T as Sync exactly when &T is Send. The compiler answers both for every type, so each type falls in one of four quadrants.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart; 6 labels.

steps.title: i32 is Send and Sync
steps.line: Auto traits: a type built from Send and Sync parts gets both.
steps.caption: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler gives them to any type built only from parts that have them. Primitives such as i32 have both, so i32 sits in the top-right quadrant. Each point sits at one fixed spot in its quadrant, so only the quadrant carries meaning.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 1 point; 4 labels. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: yes” beside i32. New in this step: i32; 4 labels.

steps.title: Rc<i32> is neither Send nor Sync
steps.line: Rc counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one.
steps.caption: Rc counts its owners with a plain integer, not an atomic one. Two threads cloning Rcs that share one count could update it at the same moment, which is undefined behaviour. So rc.rs declares Rc neither Send nor Sync, whatever it holds.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 2 points; 1 label. Note: “Send: no, Sync: no” beside Rc<i32>. New in this step: Rc<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: Cell<i32> can move but cannot be shared
steps.line: Cell::set takes &self and does no synchronisation: not Sync.
steps.caption: Cell::set takes &self and does no synchronisation, so two threads holding &Cell could write to it at once. That is why cell.rs makes Cell not Sync. It still makes Cell<T> Send whenever T is, so a whole Cell can move to another thread.
steps.picture: Quadrant chart: 3 points; 1 label. Note: “Send: yes, Sync: no” beside Cell<i32>. New in this step: Cell<i32>; 1 label.

steps.title: MutexGuard<i32> can be shared but cannot move
steps.line: Dropping it must unlock on the thread that locked: not Send.
steps.caption: Dropping a MutexGuard unlocks its mutex, and with POSIX threads a lock must be released on the thread that took it, so mutex.rs makes the guard not Send. A shared &MutexGuard gives out &i32, so mutex.rs makes the guard Sync when the value inside is Sync.
